title: Microstructural Characterization of Functionally Graded WC–17Co with an Innovative Design Manufactured by Laser Direct Energy Deposition (LDED) Technology
abstract: Abstract WC–Co is valued for its high hardness and wear resistance, but its limited toughness restricts broader applications. To address this, a unique architecture was designed where steel layers are sandwiched between WC–17Co regions to improve ductility by development of a functionally gradient structure. Laser direct energy deposition (LDED) technique as a relatively new additive manufacturing technology (AM) was employed to develop this design due to its precision and suitability for developing complex geometries. Because LDED operates on a layer-by-layer basis, it allows gradual compositional transitions, enabling the creation of a functionally graded material (FGM) that minimizes thermal mismatch and stress concentration. The resulting microstructure was examined using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). For comparative purposes, all experiments were performed on a conventional (non-FGM) LDED-processed WC–17Co sample as well. The average porosity and grain size was smaller in FGM compared to the non-FGM sample. Substantial deviations in lattice parameter of WC for the FGM sample were observed compared to the non-FGM one and reported literature for conventionally-processed WC–17Co. XRD results revealed that the FGM sample exhibits a shift in detected peaks followed by reduced residual stress than the non-graded structure, thereby decreasing the likelihood of crack initiation. The measured crystallite sizes aligned well with previously published data. While FGM sample exhibited higher hardness than non-FGM, it should also be noted that detailed analysis of mechanical properties is not within the scope of this study. This is a preliminary study only focusing on microstructural characteristics, and results could be used to explain mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties of newly developed structures in future studies.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Although LDED demonstrates promising capabilities, the fabricated parts often exhibit residual stresses and porosity, which may limit their suitability for industrial applications [ 19 ,  20 ]. In response to this challenge, Japanese researchers in the 1980s introduced the concept of functionally graded materials (FGMs), a novel category of composite materials which feature a gradual compositional and structural variation, transitioning between constituent materials. The functionally graded structure can be designed in single or multiple directions, diminishing the residual and thermal stresses generated at the interface between dissimilar materials [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 – 25 ].

Despite high hardness and wear resistance of WC–Co coatings, due to the nature of deposition techniques, it could contain high residual stress which degrades its mechanical properties and performance. In addition, presence of brittle carbide phases may restrict ductility of WC–Co coatings and, consequently, its application in the high-tech industry. To this end, it is assumed that addition of a ductile element such as steel to WC–Co in a gradual manner could improve its mechanical properties. Among technologies mentioned earlier, LDED seems to be one of the most promising methods for deposition of functionally graded WC–Co and steel. It is postulated that functionally graded WC–Co offers enhanced tunability and application versatility, while steel maintains its inherent ductile characteristics. However, if the WC–Co/Steel samples in this study were fabricated using the traditional method for developing FGM structures, then the region at the surface would mainly consist of steel material. This would have impacted its application as a wear-resistant coating. The same applies to the thermal conductivity and reverse thermal insulation in case of having steel as the major component on one side of the coating. To avoid this problem, a unique structure is designed in a way that steel is incorporated in to the core of the coating in a gradual manner. This is a novel design where several layers of functionally graded WC–Co/steel are sandwiched between two layers of graded WC–17Co.

Notwithstanding the substantial body of literature concerning FGMs generally in industry, investigations into functionally graded tungsten carbide (WC) coatings remain comparatively limited. Specifically, the utilization of the LDED method for the fabrication of functionally graded WC composites represents an underexplored domain within the scholarly community. The aim of this paper is to investigate the microstructural characteristics of this novel FGM configuration. Optical microscopy, X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning electron microscope (SEM), energy-dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) have been employed in this study. Although hardness measurements were performed to provide a general information about effect of producing a functionally graded structure on mechanical strength, the investigation of mechanical properties of newly developed structure is beyond the scope of this study. All these characteristics will be evaluated against the ones obtained from the same experiments on WC–Co part printed using the LDED process with conventional structure referred to as non-FGM. It provides a good understanding of the effect of change in the structural design in their microstructural characteristics in additively manufactured hard materials.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: The commercially available Oerlikon WOKA 3208 (Nominal composition presented in Table  1 ), with nominal particle size in the range of 40–145 μm was used as the feedstock powder for the LDED method. This powder is produced via agglomeration and sintering, yielding roughly spherical particles in which WC carbide grains with an average size of 2.5 μm are uniformly bound by the Co binder phase. The micrograph of the WOKA 3208 powder is presented in Fig.  1 . Two samples, one functionally graded material (FGM) and the other named non-functionally graded material (non-FGM), were prepared in this study. The mild steel substrate with the dimensions of 79 × 72  ×  19 mm was used for deposition of the LDED samples. The H13 powder (Plasma Powder and Systems Incorporated, PA, USA); the powder particle size ranges 44–105 μm. The chemical composition of H13 powder is as follows: 4.75–5.50 wt.% Cr; 1.10–1.75 wt.% Mo; 0.80–1.20 wt.% Si; 0.80–1.20 wt. % V; 0.32–0.45 wt.% C; 0.30 wt.% Ni, 0.25 wt.% Cu; 0.20–0.50 wt.% P; and 0.03 wt.% S, with Fe as the remainder.

sections.heading: Sample Preparation Using LDED Process
paragraphs: A laser-directed energy deposition (LDED) technique was utilized to additively manufacture both of the samples in this study. The 3D printing machine used for this purpose was an Optomec 85-R LENS by Optomec, Inc. (Albuquerque, NM, USA). The important operational printing parameters are listed in Table  2 . Table 2 Laser specifications for the LDED process Parameter Value Nominal laser power (W) 708 Maximum laser power (W)  ~ 2000 Laser spot size (mm) 2 Scanning speed (mm/s) 10.5 Hatch spacing (mm) 0.762 Shielding gas (l/min) 5 Nominal powder flow rate (g/min) 4.5

Argon with a nominal flow rate of 5 liters per minute was used as the shielding gas. The feedstock powder flow rate was approximately 4.5 grams per minute. The multi-layered configuration of the FGM sample is depicted in Fig.  1 . Both FGM and non-FGM samples were fabricated by deposition of 34 layers using a multi-bead printing approach. The actual average solidified layer height, calculated from the total deposit thickness of roughly 2.9 mm over 34 layers, is approximately 0.085 mm per layer. It is worth mentioning that FGM exhibits a gradual change in composition rather than a strictly layer-by-layer structure. It is difficult to accurately determine the composition in each layer. The schematic shown in Fig.  3  is intended only to show the general configuration of the deposition process in this study. Fig. 3 The general schematic of the multi-layer configuration in FGM sample

It is important to note that the values mentioned in Table  2  for laser power and gas flow rate were the nominal values used as set up points for deposition of the non-FGM sample. However, experimentally, the actual laser power and powder gas flow rate varied for deposition of the FGM sample due to the constant changes in composition of each layer. The laser power and gas flow rate used for deposition of each layer of the FGM sample is listed accordingly in Table  3 . Hopper 1 in Table  3  corresponds to WC–Co, while hopper 2 corresponds to H13. For brevity, details for only half of the total number of layers are listed in Table  3 , as the layers beyond layer 17 follow the same trend as layers 1–17, but in reverse order. The average grain size was estimated using the average grain intercept (AGI) method (ASTM E112-13 2021) defined as AGI = (number of intercepts)/(line length). High AGI values are indicative of materials possessing small crystal sizes, as opposed to lower values for materials with larger crystals.

In the next step, the EBSD test was conducted on both samples to determine crystallographic and grain orientation, along with phase identification. It was a complimentary test to validate results obtained from the XRD study. Due to the extreme sensitivity of EBSD to surface conditions, it is imperative to achieve the highest possible surface quality for accurate results. To ensure this, the samples were subjected to ultrasonic cleaning for 10 minutes at a temperature range of 40–45 °C. The integration of crystallographic orientation data from EBSD with elemental composition insights from EDS provided a comprehensive approach to microstructural characterization. Furthermore, Vickers hardness testing was conducted on both samples to compare their hardness values as a representative mechanical property. For this microindentation test, a load of 1000 gf and a dwell time of 10 s were applied for the microindentation test. A comprehensive analysis of their mechanical properties has been reported in a separate study [ 27 ].

sections.heading: Optical Microscopy Analysis
paragraphs: Despite the fact that functionally graded structures can mechanically mitigate the high residual stress concentration at sharp multi-material interfaces [ 7 ], Fig.  4  reveals the presence of cracks and pores in both graded and non-graded samples. These images were taken from the cross-section, illustrating the middle section along with portions of top and bottom regions. Figure  4 (c) and (d) shows smaller regions of the microstructure at higher magnification. Three distinct contrasts can be observed in Fig.  4 (c), whereas only two contrasts can be identified in microstructure of non-FGM sample shown in Fig.  4 (d). Further elemental composition examinations presented in the next section, confirms that the three contrasts in Fig.  4 (c) correspond to WC, Co, and Fe while Fig.  4 (d) shows only WC and Co. sections.heading: SEM/EDS Analysis
paragraphs: Figure  5  presents the SEM micrograph of the FGM sample which is divided into three distinguishable regions, corresponding to the graded WC-17Co layers at the top (Region 3), middle (Region 2), and bottom (Region 1). As shown in Table  5 , preliminary EDS results indicated that region 3 has the highest WC-Co content, while region 2 is composed of deposited steel layers. It must be noted that similar distinction of regions was considered for non-FGM sample for the reason of comparison. It should be noted that the SEM image presented in this micrograph was taken from a cross-section parallel to the build direction. Elemental composition analysis was performed for all three regions, which were approximately defined based on the layer configuration shown in Fig.  5 . It is worth mentioning that Table  5  does not rank regions based on Fe content, instead it highlights the elements present in each region. The regions are listed in numerical order. Fig. 5 The SEM micrograph showing all three regions identified with the microstructure of the FGM sample Table 5 Elemental composition [Wt. %] of the FGM specimen analyzed using SEM-EDS, corresponding to regions illustrated in Fig.  5 Region C O Co Fe W 1 3.7 ± 1.1 1.1 ± 0.8 7.2 ± 2.6 50.8 ± 3.3 37.1 ± 8.1 2 5.3 ± 0.9 5.50 ± 1.2 8.9 ± 2.1 52.1 ± 5.1 28.1 ± 5.7 3 7.6 ± 1.4 1.7 ± 0.6 10.5 ± 2.6 2.5 ± 1.9 77.7 ± 8.9

The Fe content in region 1 is substantially high, primarily due to the large diffusion and migration of iron atoms from the substrate into the deposited layer in this region. Obviously, the intensity of the migration of Fe atoms decreases moving toward the core and top regions. This phenomenon has previously been reported in the literature for additively manufactured WC samples [ 10 ,  11 ].

The results from the hardness measurements are illustrated in Fig.  6 . The findings clearly indicate the existence of three separate regions characterized by distinct hardness values. The overall hardness, when averaged across all layers, was higher in the FGM sample than in the non-FGM sample. All regions in FGM sample exhibited higher local hardness compared to the ones in non-FGM sample with exception of region 2 (the middle layer) that higher hardness was measured in the non-FGM sample. Additionally, the porosity measurement of the FGM sample for regions 1, 2, and 3 yielded values of 5.55  ± 0.67 %, 6.69  ± 0.34 %, and 5.42  ± 0.59 %, respectively. Laser power has been reported to have a direct impact on the evolution of porosity and cracks during LDED printing. An increase in laser power leads to binder evaporation that increases the number of pores and cracks in the region [ 16 ]. As shown in Table  3 , the laser power increases from layer 1 to layer 17, a direct consequence of which can be seen as an increase in porosity from region 1 to region 2. For the non-FGM sample, on the other hand, the laser power is not increased with layers; therefore, all three regions show almost constant porosities. Fig. 6 Average hardness measured for the three main layers in ( a ) FGM and ( b ) non-FGM samples

For the non-FGM sample, the corresponding values of 6.34 , ± 0.58, 6.39  ± 0.16 %, and 6.66  ± 0.45 % were determined in the same regions, respectively. As displayed in Fig.  4 , the hardness value of the FGM sample in region 1 is slightly larger than the non-FGM sample, which might be due to the smaller grain size and slightly lower porosity of the FGM sample. Region 2 of the FGM sample, however, shows a lower hardness value than the non-FGM one, that can be attributed to the higher Fe content and slightly higher porosity in the FGM sample. Moreover, the region 3 (top) in the FGM sample exhibited increased hardness relative to that of the non-FGM sample, which may stem from smaller WC grain (particle) size in the FGM sample as previously seen in Fig.  4 . In addition to smaller carbide size, slightly lower porosity in this region of the FGM sample compared to the non-FGM sample could also contribute to the observed higher hardness values.

A distinctive microstructural characteristic of the LDED process is the substantial diversity in grain dimensions, geometry, morphology, and crystallographic orientations [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. As shown in Fig.  7 , microstructural features such as porosity, cracks, and compositional distribution vary considerably in FGM and non-FGM samples. The FGM image shows fewer, smaller pores distributed across the microstructure. These pores appear more isolated, indicating a relatively uniform density and better bonding. Fig. 7 SEM images of ( a ) FGM and ( b ) non-FGM WC-17Co samples

In contrast, the non-FGM sample displays a higher density of pores, including some larger ones. The pores are more concentrated near specific regions, particularly at grain boundaries or along the layers, which can be attributed to weak interfacial bonding or defects during the material processing [ 28 ]. Black regions observed in both specimens result from surface contamination generated during the grinding process. Due to the temperature gradient extending from the core of molten pool to its outer boundary, an interfacial tension gradient (termed Marangoni stress) arises which can serve as a significant driver for convective currents. This convective heat transfer often dominates thermal flow within the fusion zone, influencing its overall shape and dimensions [ 29 ].

The FGM structure shows minimal evidence of long cracks, and the cracks present are finer and less continuous. Nonetheless, the non-FGM structure exhibits a prominent large central crack, which extends vertically. The initiation of these cracks can be attributed to process-inherent thermal gradient, stress accumulation and pronounced thermo-mechanical property misalignments across deposited material interfaces [ 30 ]. Residual stress intensifies as the distance from the substrate grows, resulting in the buildup of dislocations. This observation aligns with the literature findings [ 7 ].

Region 3 of the FGM sample, shown in Fig.  8  (a), exhibits distinct phases and a more complex grain morphology compared to the non-FGM sample in Fig.  8  (b). These differences are most likely induced by thermal gradient and solidification behavior during LDED process. As previously reported in the literature [ 30 ], melt pool formation can influence grain growth orientation, with rapid cooling near the substrate promoting fine equiaxed grains, while the upper regions exhibit columnar grains due to thermally driven epitaxial growth [ 31 ] . Fig. 8 Secondary dendritic arm spacing (SDAS) for region 3 (top region) ( a ) FGM and ( b ) non-FGM specimen

SDAS, as a fundamental microstructural descriptor of solidification processes, reflects cooling dynamics, with smaller values indicating rapid solidification, as is the case with the LDED process. Lower SDAS leads to grain refinement, lower porosity in inter-dendritic regions, and ultimately mechanical strength [ 25 ]. This enhancement can be attributed to inhibition of dislocation motion by smaller values of SDAS. The obtained SDAS values for region 3 (top region) of the FGM and non-FGM samples are presented in Fig.  6 . The lines displayed in Fig.  8  represent 11 randomly selected sets for SDAS measurements. The average values for the 11 dendritic grains selected for the FGM and non-FGM were 0.964 and 1.557 µm, respectively.

Figure  9  shows a sample of high-resolution micrographs used for the EDS experiment of the FGM sample. The regions with light contrast correspond to WC grains, known for their high hardness and angular morphology, whereas, the darker matrix between the WC particles is likely the cobalt binder, which holds the WC grains together. Some of the dark regions may also include steel or other secondary metallic inclusions, potentially introduced during processing. Fig. 9 Marking locations denote where EDS analysis was performed corresponding to Table  6  on ( a ) FGM and ( b ) non-FGM samples

The resulting elemental compositions for each marked spectrum are reported in Table  6 . The results indicate migration of steel from substrate to coating that has been further supported by Azarmi et al. [ 11 ] in their study as well. However, Co content is observed more in the FGM sample compared to the non-FGM one. This can be attributed to the diffusion and intermixing from the substrate. sections.heading: X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) Analysis
Analysis of Grain and Crystallite Size
paragraphs: The average grain intercept (AGI) method was used to evaluate the particle sizes in FGM and non-FGM samples and investigate the effect of processing techniques on these values, considering the identical original WC-17Co feedstock powder for both specimens. Figure  11  demonstrates a representative example of how grain size was calculated for the FGM specimen. The corresponding results for the region 3 of both samples are presented in Table  7 . The region 3 has been selected owing to the fact that the region 3 surface dictates service behavior, effectiveness, and service life of the component in applications which are subjected to fracture, wear, thermal stress, fatigue, etc. In addition, the region 3 is less affected by migration of substrate material as indicated in this study and a previous report on the same material [ 11 ]. The average grain size over the total area within the microstructure for the FGM and non-FGM samples were calculated as 4.1 ± 0.7 and 5.9 ± 0.9 µm, respectively. Fig. 11 Representative example of grain size measurements in region 3 of the FGM sample Table 7 Comparative particle size analysis of tungsten carbide in FGM and non-FGM specimens Maximum carbide particle size, µm Average carbide particle size, µm FGM Non-FGM 14.6 19.9 4.9 ± 0.4 6.4 ± 0.7

The finer grains can be attributed to the different cooling rates in samples. The refinement in the FGM sample primarily stems from the superior thermal conductivity of tungsten carbide (WC), which improves the heat removal and consequently accelerates the cooling process during solidification. This heightened cooling rate impedes grain coarsening and leads to finer overall grain sizes.

The crystallite size evaluations for the WC yielded 296.5 ± 30.3 Å and 292.7 ± 45.3 Å for FGM and non-FGM samples, respectively. It is interesting to note that the FGM sample has a slightly larger crystallite size than the non-FGM one, while the average grain size and SDAS were both larger in the non-FGM sample. However, the crystallite sizes calculated here correspond well with the measured lattice parameters found from the XRD experiment. The measured crystallite sizes in this study are also in good agreement with the ones previously reported for LPBF-processed WC-17Co in the literature [ 34 ].

sections.heading: Electron Backscatter Diffraction (EBSD)
Conclusion
paragraphs: It is important to know that the developed FGM structure showed enhanced properties (e.g., hardness) without major changes in the microstructure of the WC-17Co processed by LDED technology. A concurrent study showed advanced mechanical properties that make the FGM sample more suitable to be used as wear-resistant coatings, thermal barriers, and aerospace components, outperforming the non-FGM structures in demanding environments. The mechanical properties were not in the scope of this work and will be presented as a separate study in future.
